meta.primarySource: J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 2026 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, 30th Annual Edition. USD assumption matrix.
meta.returnBasis: nominal, compound (geometric), net of fees where the source states it
meta.note: Not one number below was produced by this project. Every return, volatility and correlation is read from the J.P. Morgan matrix cited above. J.P. Morgan revises these every year and has revised them by more than a percentage point in a single year. They are a considered view, not a fact. J.P. Morgan published its 2027 edition on 19 October 2026, but its full matrix of volatilities and correlations is not public yet, so this tool keeps the complete 2026 edition rather than mixing the two.

crossChecks.name: Vanguard Capital Markets Model, 10-year annualised, simulation date 30 September 2026
crossChecks.examples: US equities 4.8 to 6.8 percent, developed markets outside the US 5.3 to 7.3 percent, emerging markets 3.7 to 5.7 percent, US aggregate bonds 5.1 to 6.1 percent.

crossChecks.name: BlackRock Investment Institute capital market assumptions, data as of 30 June 2026
crossChecks.examples: US large cap 8.97 percent, emerging large cap 8.80 percent, global aggregate bonds hedged 4.51 percent.

crossChecks.name: UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2026 (Dimson, Marsh, Staunton), 1900 to 2025
crossChecks.examples: US equities 6.6 percent real per year and 9.8 percent nominal over 126 years. US bonds 1.6 percent real. US bills 0.5 percent real. Gold 1.3 percent real since 1900.

meta.disagreement: On emerging markets equity, J.P. Morgan said 7.8 percent (2026 edition; 7.1 in its 2027 edition), BlackRock says 8.8 percent, and Vanguard says 3.7 to 5.7 percent. That spread is about five percentage points a year on the same asset class over the same horizon. Anyone who tells you the expected return of an asset class to one decimal place is telling you about their model, not about the future.

assetClasses.label: Cash and Treasury bills
assetClasses.plain: Money you can spend tomorrow. Earns a little, loses to inflation slowly.

assetClasses.label: Short government bonds
assetClasses.plain: Lending to the US government for a few years. Safer than shares, pays more than cash.

assetClasses.label: Global bonds, currency hedged
assetClasses.plain: Lending to governments around the world, with the currency risk stripped out.

assetClasses.label: Inflation-linked bonds
assetClasses.plain: Government bonds whose payments rise with US inflation. Protects purchasing power, not price.

assetClasses.label: Global shares
assetClasses.plain: Part ownership of thousands of companies worldwide. The main engine of long-run growth.

assetClasses.label: Emerging market shares
assetClasses.plain: Companies in faster-growing, less stable economies. Higher expected return, bigger swings.

assetClasses.label: Listed property
assetClasses.plain: Shares in companies that own and rent out buildings. Behaves mostly like shares, not like a house.

assetClasses.label: Gold
assetClasses.plain: Owned by no government and issued by no bank. Pays you nothing and can go nowhere for a decade.

historical.title: What these actually returned, historically
historical.note: The forecasts above are what large houses think the next ten to fifteen years will look like. The numbers below are what actually happened over the longest periods anyone has measured. They are much higher. Both are real, and the gap between them is the most honest thing on this page: nobody knows which one the next thirty years will resemble.
historical.primarySource: UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2026, compiled by Dimson, Marsh and Staunton, covering 1900 to 2025

lines.label: Global shares
lines.measures: Dimson Marsh Staunton developed markets composite, in dollars

lines.label: Emerging market shares
lines.measures: Dimson Marsh Staunton emerging markets composite, in dollars. Over the full 1900 to 2025 period it was 6.9 percent, held back by markets that shut down entirely in the first half of the century.

lines.label: Listed property
lines.measures: FTSE Nareit All Equity REITs, total return. Over the last thirty years it was 9.42 percent.

lines.label: Global bonds
lines.measures: Dimson Marsh Staunton US long government bonds. No verified global bond figure was published for this period, so the US series stands in for it.

lines.label: Short government bonds
lines.measures: Same US long bond series. Short bonds would have earned less than this and more than cash.

lines.label: Inflation-linked bonds
lines.measures: These did not exist until 1997, so there is no long history. The bond figure stands in for them.

lines.label: Cash and Treasury bills
lines.measures: Dimson Marsh Staunton US Treasury bills. Half a percent a year above inflation, over 126 years.

lines.label: Gold
lines.measures: The only published figure is the real one, 1.3 percent a year above inflation. The 4.2 percent shown is that figure plus the 2.9 percent inflation the same source reports for the same period. That addition is our arithmetic, not theirs.

landmarks.label: US shares, every year since 1900
landmarks.sub: 6.6 percent a year after inflation. One dollar became 124,854.

landmarks.label: The S&P 500, last 50 years
landmarks.sub: The number most people have in their head when they say shares return about ten percent.

landmarks.label: Cash since 1900
landmarks.sub: 0.5 percent a year after inflation. Cash barely keeps up, over 126 years.

cashErosion.label: What holding dollars in cash has cost since 2019
cashErosion.measures: US CPI for All Urban Consumers, not seasonally adjusted, 1982-84 = 100. October 2019 is the month Lebanon's banking crisis began. This measures what a dollar buys in the United States. It is not a measure of the cost of living in Lebanon, which moved differently.
cashErosion.source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index news releases
cashErosion.caution: Do not state this as a general rule. Long-run US inflation is nearer 3 percent a year. The last six years ran hotter than the long run.
